# Unit B, phase 1: the new text's assertions, one per sentence

### 14.4 One plan, two ways to apply it
- V1 A resolved condition (the path-addressed sparse overlay that sets a build's state) is applied two ways, because a one-shot service and an iterating one want different things from the same validated list of condition entries (D-066). [D-066]
- V2 The section gives the two ways, then the read-selector family.

#### Applying a plan
- V3 All string work, validation and addressing are functions of the shape of the condition.
- V4 Every hot path holds the shape fixed while varying values.
- V5 Execution is therefore resolve-once/execute-many.
- V6 A valid list of condition entries compiles two ways, one for each way to apply it.
- V7 Specialized `apply!` serves the service that iterates, trim's per-evaluation write (D-066). [D-066] (bold)
- V8 Its plan holds, per leaf, a lens (the compiled navigation step of a condition entry), a destination and a converter.
- V9 It unrolls stores through the baked lenses and converters.
- V10 Those are the same machine operations as FlightCore's in-place state writes, with no allocation, no strings and no dispatch.
- V11 The per-iteration shape check is the mechanism of §9.5 transferred. [§9.5]
- V12 The tree type is proven by dispatch, and it carries the full nesting, every field name and leaf type.
- V13 A `===` comparison of each prefix string closes the remainder.
- V14 `===` on strings compares content, so a prefix computed at run time pairs with the compiled one exactly as a literal does, at the cost of one short comparison per `at` node.
- V15 Shape drift is a tree of another type, or a prefix that differs at a position.
- V16 It is `ConditionShapeDrift` (Appendix C), reason `:tree_type` or `:prefix`, a structured error rather than silent corruption. [Appendix C]
- V17 The cost is Julia codegen once per condition shape, and it grows with the shape's writes (D-066). [D-066]
- V18 On Julia 1.13 it measures 10 to 50 ms up to 32 writes, 0.09 s at 64 and 0.2 s at 128 (`docs/reports/20261002_tuple_walks/`).
- V19 That cost is noise against the model's own first-sweep warmup (seconds).
- V20 It is paid once per tree type per session, so it spreads over every evaluation of every trim of that shape, an envelope of trims included.
- V21 The dynamic walk serves the one-shot uses, `init!`, `linearize`'s operating condition and trim's setup write (§14.8, D-066). [§14.8, D-066] (bold)
- V22 It executes the same validated condition entries by runtime dispatch per write, from a plan that holds the converted values themselves.
- V23 That takes microseconds in total, with allocation permitted, since the stopped-sim path was never under the zero-alloc regime (§9.8). [§9.8]
- V24 It needs no per-shape codegen.
- V25 Fifty structurally different scripted conditions cost fifty walks, not fifty compiles.
- V26 Which of the two a service uses is internal, never user-facing API.
- V27 The per-iteration ledger for trim has four terms.
- V28 They are the user fragment math, the leaf stores, the folded shape check and the sweep (one pass through the execution order against the current state).
- V29 The fragment math is the domain computations, unchanged from Flight.jl's, plus building the tree, which allocates nothing (§14.2). [§14.2]
- V30 The sweep dominates, exactly as `f_ode!` does in FlightCore, where it is the continuous-dynamics function a model extends.

#### The read-selector family
- V31 The read-selector family is closed (D-095). [D-095] (bold)
- V32 Its members are `get_state(path, leaf)`, `get_deriv(path, leaf)`, `get_output(path, leaf)`, `get_input(leaf)` and `get_face(leaf)`.
- V33 They form one address space for every reader of the model.
- V34 `leaf` is a leaf address (D-276). [D-276] (bold)
- V35 It is the field or face name (the name a port wears on its component's boundary), followed by `.name` and `[k]` or `[k,l]` steps in any order, as in `"pose.q_eb[2]"`, `"ω_eb_b[1]"` or `"J[1,3]"`.
- V36 A bare `Symbol` is the short form of a plain name, so `get_state("kin", :θ)` reads `get_state("kin", "θ")` (D-276). [D-276] (bold)
- V37 A face name is an arbitrary string and may contain a dot (§8.6), so on `get_input` and `get_face` the head is matched rather than parsed. [§8.6]
- V38 The head is the longest declared face name that is a prefix of the address and is followed by the end, a `.` or a `[`.
- V39 A `Symbol` leaf names the face whole, with no steps.
- V40 So `get_input("wing.throttle")` and `get_input("wind[1]")` both resolve, and where faces `a` and `a.b` both exist, `"a.b"` names the face `a.b`.
- V41 Each step is checked at resolution against the type resolved so far (D-276). [D-276] (bold)
- V42 A `.name` step needs an isbits struct with that field.
- V43 An index step needs an `SArray`, with one index or one per dimension, and a vector leaf thereby yields named scalars.
- V44 A step never enters an opaque leaf (a field handle or a `Symbol`), which is read whole.
- V45 `get_deriv`, and `get_state` on the continuous tier, take at most an index step, since a continuous state field is flat (§7.1, D-276). [§7.1, D-276] (bold)
- V46 A discrete `s` field is isbits or a `Symbol` (§3.2), and `get_state` on it takes the full address. [§3.2]
- V47 The address is checked once and baked, and the read runs as field loads and indexing unrolled at compile time (D-276). [D-276] (bold)
- V48 The names carry a deliberate `get_` prefix (D-095). [D-095]
- V49 A selector is a deferred read, a value describing the read the compiled gather will perform.
- V50 The prefix names that action, and it keeps five short common nouns out of the namespace user declarations share with domain code.
- V51 There is no selector for a value a component computes without declaring it, and there cannot be one, because only declared cells and stores are addressable (§4.2, §8.3). [§4.2, §8.3]
- V52 So a reader that wants one is asking the producing component to declare it an output (§8.3). [§8.3]
- V53 A service evaluation needing an undeclared intermediate has that one remedy too, and it is the same for every client.
- V54 The component exports it (§14.7). [§14.7]
- V55 `get_face` addresses an output face of the mount level, the level its read set is mounted at (§14.9, D-277). [§14.9, D-277]
- V56 Mounting relocates a whole problem or tap set (the three selector lists declaring what linearization seeds and reports) with `at(prefix, …)`.
- V57 At the root that face is root-exported.
- V58 Either way the read is an integration read (§11.2). [§11.2]
- V59 A selector resolves against a source, before any client policy applies (D-098). [D-098] (bold)
- V60 The table selectors (`get_output`, `get_input`, `get_face`) resolve against a table source.
- V61 A table source is a boundary snapshot, or the scratch tables a service evaluation instantiates (§14.8, D-124). [§14.8, D-124]
- V62 The store selectors (`get_state`, `get_deriv`) resolve only against live stores (D-098). [D-098]
- V63 The table/store axis separates table-borne values from store-borne ones, not snapshots from services.
- V64 Only stopped-sim service evaluations, `checkpoint`, and post-run inspection of the live stores (the replay-to-inspect) ever hold live stores (§11.2). [§11.2]
- V65 The snapshot deliberately carries no state stores (§11.2), and `ẋ` buffers are integrator scratch, not boundary-consistent objects outside a service evaluation. [§11.2]
- V66 A reader resolving for a table source that names a store selector is therefore refused at resolution, as a `ReadResolution` with reason `:store_selector` (D-406). [D-406]
- V67 The resolver takes the source it resolves for, so the rule is the resolver's and not a client's (D-406). [D-406] (bold)
- V68 The honest remedy (§11.2) is to declare the field in `y_types`, return it from `y_state`, and read the resulting port (§5.3). [§11.2, §5.3]
- V69 On top of the source rule sits one piece of authoring guidance (D-414). [D-414]
- V70 A service read, trim's `reads` or a tap, that should outlive the build reads a face with `get_face` (D-125). [D-125]
- V71 `get_face` resolves through export chains exactly as mounting resolves root input faces (§14.9), so the read side mirrors the write side. [§14.9]
- V72 An inspection read, a binding's or `series`', may name any cell the structure has, since it promises nothing beyond this build (D-083). [D-083]
- V73 Both resolve under the one service walk (§13.3). [§13.3]
- V74 Trim's `reads` and linearization's taps name `get_state`/`get_deriv`/`get_output`/`get_input`/`get_face`.
- V75 They do so within the scopes the locality law (§6.1) and fragment scoping (§14.2) describe, as authoring guidance (D-414). [§6.1, §14.2, D-414]
- V76 An equilibrium equation meant to outlive the build it was posed against therefore binds the curated face behind a generically held child (one held through a non-concrete field type) rather than a path into it.
- V77 Inspection reads admit the whole family, within the source rule.
- V78 Output-device bindings and log extraction by `series` take deep paths, `get_face` names and leaf addresses alike (D-406, D-407, D-414). [D-406, D-407, D-414]
- V79 Snapshot inspection reads a cell by path and port name instead (§11.2). [§11.2]
- V80 A store selector resolves only for a reader that runs over live stores, which today are the services' (§14.7, §14.10). [§14.7, §14.10]
- V81 A snapshot-bound reader is barred from it by source, not by client.
- V82 `ignore_stop_requests` is not a family client.
- V83 It names requesters from the `Build`'s requester roster (the build's list of stop requests, one per `StopFlag` output port), period (§13.5, D-316). [§13.5, D-316]
- V84 Termination is run policy over the requests the model declares, and no path selector reaches `ignore_stop_requests` (D-060). [D-060]
- V85 The five selectors and their sources:
- V86 `get_state(path, leaf)`
- V87 live stores
- V88 `get_deriv(path, leaf)`
- V89 live stores
- V90 `get_output(path, leaf)`
- V91 a table source
- V92 `get_input(leaf)`
- V93 a table source
- V94 `get_face(leaf)`
- V95 a table source
- V96 Compiled readers are the gather twin (D-066) over this family and the layout tables (where each value physically lives). [D-066] (bold)
- V97 Trim's residual reads (`ẋ` and output fields) and linearization's Jacobian gather are one primitive run in reverse.
- V98 It is one machinery, in both directions, in the `Build`'s client kit.
- V99 A compiled plan or reader carries the activation it was compiled at and applies only to a store set of that activation.
- V100 That pairing is a framework invariant the services uphold, not a user-facing check.
- V101 Neither plans nor readers are user values.
- V102 `apply!` ends at established stores.
- V103 Making the model coherent is the job of boundary zero (the initialization boundary, the ordinary macro-sequence with an empty integrate), which §14.5 specifies. [§14.5]

### 14.5 Boundary zero: an ordinary boundary with authored incoming transitions
- V104 `apply!` establishes the stores at `t₀`.
- V105 The init service then completes the §10.6 macro-sequence with an empty integrate (D-067). [§10.6, D-067] (bold)
- V106 The sequence is the following.
- V107 > project → [sweep → guards → handlers]\ → due `s_update` calls → first snapshot
- V108 After the first snapshot `init!` takes the trace header, the checkpoint (the `Model`'s state at a frame top as one value) of the state the sequence leaves (§11.5, D-274). [§11.5, D-274]
- V109 The parity with an ordinary boundary is exact, not approximate.
- V110 The pieces follow one by one, in run order.
- V111 Projection, the sweep, events and the due `s_update` calls come first, then the `t₀` argument, then what boundary zero (the initialization boundary at `t₀`) means for trim.
- V112 Project runs.
- V113 Authored `x` can sit off-manifold.
- V114 A hand-assembled quaternion may be ulps off unit norm, or a condition (the path-addressed sparse overlay that sets a build's state) may write part of a constrained block against fresh defaults.
- V115 Projection after condition writes holds the same position it holds after any other `x` mutation.
- V116 And it costs nothing when the state is already clean.
- V117 The sweep runs, and every discrete output stage publishes, due or not (D-205). [D-205] (bold)
- V118 `t₀` is a grid point of every phase-free divisor, so the `Φ = 0` components are due in full.
- V119 An offset component (§10.5) is not due, because its first tick is at `Φ·Δt_base`. [§10.5]
- V120 Its output stages run at boundary zero all the same, publishing from the authored `s` and the `t₀` table in the ordinary sorted walk.
- V121 That evaluation is establishment, not a scheduled sample.
- V122 The schedule owns every instant after `t₀`, and the first sample the component's `s_update` consumes remains its `Φ·Δt_base` tick's.
- V123 What the rule buys is a `t₀` snapshot carrying the authored world fully evaluated.
- V124 No published cell holds the probe's synthesized values.
- V125 That is the §14.6 barrier extended from the root inputs to the whole table. [§14.6]
- V126 Events run.
- V127 A condition can land a guard predicate in holding territory (firing on not-holding → holding transitions, never bare sign changes).
- V128 An authored stall flag, or a strut authored into contact, does exactly that.
- V129 The event then fires visibly at `t₀` rather than one step later.
- V130 The prior rule grounds that timing (§10.6, D-292). [§10.6, D-292]
- V131 Boundary zero establishes every guard prior (the event's stored predicate sample from the previous boundary) as not-holding.
- V132 Suppressing those firings was rejected (D-067), on the lesson of the stage-on-interaction rule (§11.7). [D-067, §11.7]
- V133 That lesson is that insurance masking invariant violations is anti-diagnostic (D-026). [D-026]
- V134 The trace header is taken after the sequence (§11.5). [§11.5]
- V135 Replay restores it and runs no boundary zero, so whatever fired at `t₀` comes back as part of the restored state and never fires twice (§12.7, D-274). [§12.7, D-274]
- V136 The checkpoint records the post-firing state faithfully and suppresses nothing.
- V137 A stop request already reading `STOP_REQUESTED` is a different category.
- V138 Nothing fires.
- V139 The request simply holds in the published `t₀` snapshot and the loop reacts (§13.5, D-413). [§13.5, D-413]
- V140 Due `s_update` calls run.
- V141 This follows from an interval-alignment fact that is easy to mis-picture.
- V142 It is hereby a taught contract, sibling to the boundary-sampling line (§8.6). [§8.6]
- V143 A boundary's `s_update` is the outgoing transition (D-067). [D-067] (bold)
- V144 At tick `t_k` it consumes the completed boundary's samples and produces `s_{k+1}`, the value the next tick reads.
- V145 The transition that carried `s` into `t_k` ran at `t_{k-1}`.
- V146 Boundary zero is missing its incoming transitions on both tiers (the continuous and discrete sides of the hybrid formalism), and authorship replaces both.
- V147 discrete
- V148 the `s_update` that would have produced a discrete leaf's `s(0)` never ran; the condition authored `s(0)`
- V149 `s_update` consumes the `t₀` samples and produces `s(1)`
- V150 the gated stages read `s(1)`
- V151 continuous
- V152 the integration over `[t_{-1}, t_0]` that would have produced a continuous leaf's `x(0)` never ran; the condition authored `x(0)`
- V153 the authored `x(0)` is the initial condition of the outgoing integrate, $t_0 \to t_0 + h$
- V154 The outgoing work all runs, and `t₀`'s `s_update` has its only opportunity.
- V155 `s(1)` must sit in the store before `t₁`'s gated stages read it.
- V156 An accumulator $s_{k+1} = s_k + \Delta t \, e_k$ authored with $s_0 = 0$ under nonzero $e(t_0)$ would otherwise first integrate $e(t_1)$, putting the whole sampled-data lattice one period late (D-067). [D-067]
- V157 The authored `s(0)` needs no protection, because it is published in the `t₀` snapshot regardless.
- V158 The continuous-tier analogue of `s_update`-at-`t₀` is not the empty incoming integrate but that first outgoing one.
- V159 Both authored values are the published initial conditions of their outgoing transitions.
- V160 `t₀` is an init-service argument (default `0.0`), never a condition entry, because time is not a store of any component (D-067). [D-067] (bold)
- V161 The harmonic grid (every discrete period an integer multiple of `Δt_base`) anchors at whatever `t₀` boundary zero runs at.
- V162 Both init-service entry points carry the argument, with the same default (D-110). [D-110] (bold)
- V163 They are `init!(model, condition; t0)` and `trim!`'s commit (§14.8, D-319). [§14.8, D-319]
- V164 The simulation's `init!(sim, condition; t0)` wraps the model's, resolving the condition and opening the run before the model's method writes.
- V165 Each form of `trim!` commits through the matching `init!`, the model's or the simulation's (§14.8). [§14.8]
- V166 Conditions are time-free.
- V167 Nothing after boundary zero sets the origin.
- V168 A restore inherits the clock and takes no `t0` (D-273). [D-273]
- V169 Trim is untouched by all of this (D-067). [D-067] (bold)
- V170 Optimizer iterations are raw write → sweep → read cycles on the activation, with no boundaries, no events and no `s_update`.
- V171 Only the committed solution executes boundary zero.
- V172 A guard firing at commit is a wanted failure signal.
- V173 The hand-written trim asserts of Flight.jl's Cessna 172 models (`!stall`, no weight-on-wheels, `ω > ω_idle`) become the model's own event logic, surfaced through the ordinary machinery instead of `@assert`.
- V174 A handler that fires at commit moves the committed stores off the solved point.
- V175 Saying nothing would be warn-but-assign relocated.
- V176 The channel that says it is the trim report (§14.8, D-126). [§14.8, D-126] (bold)
- V177 A commit-fired handler is not the only mover, and the second one is unconditional (D-155). [D-155] (bold)
- V178 Boundary zero's first act is `x_projection`, so the committed `x` is `x_projection(x)`, not the solver's `x`.
- V179 An attitude quaternion renormalized by a few ulps is the canonical case.
- V180 That move is legitimate, wanted, and usually invisible in the residuals.
- V181 But the point the stores sit at is no longer the point the verdict was read at.
- V182 Both movers take the same remedy, specified with the report in §14.8. [§14.8]

### 14.6 Root-input totality: the missing-value error and the `override` combinator
- V183 Root inputs are the one initialized datum without declared defaults.
- V184 That is the bare-types decision (§11.3), upheld here (D-068, D-376). [§11.3, D-068, D-376]
- V185 So a root input's only source before boundary zero is the condition (the path-addressed sparse overlay that sets a build's state).
- V186 Boundary zero is the initialization boundary, the ordinary macro-sequence with an empty integrate.
- V187 Three consequences follow.
- V188 They are the totality check, the probe-value barrier, and baselines layered by `override`.
- V189 Totality is a precondition of starting, checked by the service (D-068). [D-068] (bold)
- V190 A condition value is legitimately partial.
- V191 Fragments compose, and trim iterations write subsets.
- V192 So "every root input covered" is not a property of conditions.
- V193 Totality is a property of every application that establishes a complete world over virgin stores (D-149). [D-149] (bold)
- V194 That principle, not an enumeration, names the sites.
- V195 They are `init!`, trim's setup application to freshly allocated scratch stores, trim's commit through boundary zero (§14.8), and linearization's operating condition under `about`, applied to its own scratch (§14.10). [§14.8, §14.10]
- V196 That is one class, one mechanism and one kind.
- V197 Each compares the resolved plan's root-input coverage against the `Build`'s `input_faces` before writing anything.
- V198 A shortfall is one collected, declaration-ordered diagnostic (`UninitializedInputs`, Appendix C) naming every uncovered face. [Appendix C]
- V199 Coverage is a plan-level fact, because both operands are resolution-time data.
- V200 The check is therefore one comparison, and it runs before any evaluation, not merely before any write.
- V201 Pre-write means all-or-nothing.
- V202 A rejected init leaves the sim exactly as it was, the same posture as failed trim.
- V203 The probe-value barrier is structural (D-068). [D-068] (bold)
- V204 The `probe_value` synthesis (zero, false, the first enum value or `T()`) exists so build-time probes can exercise code with fabricated inputs (§9.3). [§9.3]
- V205 A fabricated zero is a fine probe input and a terrible flight condition.
- V206 A silently zeroed `mixture` kills the engine and sends the user debugging aerodynamics.
- V207 The services path simply contains no call to it.
- V208 A root input gets a condition value or the application errors, with no third branch.
- V209 Replay likewise never synthesizes.
- V210 The trace header holds every root-input cell as boundary zero left it, and with totality enforced that record is complete by construction.
- V211 That discharges the requirement (§11.3). [§11.3]
- V212 Baselines are aircraft-shipped condition functions, layered by `override` (D-068). [D-068] (bold)
- V213 Nobody hand-writes ~20 root-input values per script.
- V214 In Flight.jl the `@kwdef` defaults of `SystemsInitializer`, the systems initializer of its Cessna 172 model (`c172.jl`), carry that load.
- V215 Their successor is ordinary user math in one authoritative home, such as `ready_for_taxi(ac)` or `cold_and_dark(ac)`, returning full-coverage conditions.
- V216 But "baseline plus tweaks" collides with the duplicate-leaf error (§14.2) by design. [§14.2]
- V217 The collision is the intent, and the fourth node kind, `override(base, patch)`, exists for it (D-068). [D-068] (bold)
- V218 It is ordered and asymmetric, where `combine` is symmetric and collision-intolerant.
- V219 At resolution a leaf present in both takes the patch's value, and the origin names both layers.
- V220 Collisions within one layer remain errors.
- V221 Variadic layering (`override(campaign, aircraft, todays_case)`) composes.
- V222 Trim uses it on day one.
- V223 The committed condition is `override(baseline, condition(d))`, the solved condition over full coverage (D-068). [D-068]
